newsitem.title: GERMANY: Degussa admits melting down Jewish gold.
newsitem.headline: Degussa admits melting down Jewish gold.

text.p: Germany's Degussa AG, one of the world's largest metals firms, acknowledged on Saturday that it had melted down gold and silver taken from Holocaust victims during the Nazi era.
"During National Socialist (Nazi) times, Jewish citizens in Germany and in neighbouring occupied countries were forced to give up gold, silver and other precious metals," Degussa said in a statement.
"Most of the materials -- plate silver, jewellery, old silver, and silver and gold fragments -- was refined at Degussa."
Asked for clarification of what Degussa meant by "fragments", a spokeswoman for the firm said: "We didn't know ... we were not forced to ask where it came from."
As far as it knew, the precious metals came from the Reichsbank, Germany's then central bank, and from state pawnbrokers, the firm said.
The metals and chemicals company said it had melted down the gold and silver under orders from the state and had been paid state agreed fees for the work.

Degussa is the latest in a growing list of German companies -- including insurer Allianz, railway Deutsche Bahn AG, carmaker Volkswagen AG and Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank -- taking a fresh look at the role they played in Nazi atrocities of the 1930s and 1940s.

The new efforts were sparked partly by growing public pressure on firms to reveal the less savoury aspects of the history, and by a recent multi-billion-dollar lawsuit in the United States which alleged that German insurer Allianz AG, among others, cheated Holocaust survivors of their assets.

Allianz said on Friday that it had asked an American historian to research its historical relationship with the Nazi regime. The insurer has also set up hotlines in Germany and the U.S. to assist claimants.

A senior Degussa official, Michael Jansen, said in the statement the firm was well aware of its past and, in efforts to compensate for it, was a major supporter of numerous Jewish institutions in Israel, the United States and Germany.
"We have never made a secret of our past," he said.
Degussa said it had now agreed with the World Jewish Congress to investigate further its role in the disappearance of Jewish-owned precious metals during the Third Reich.
It was also engaged in a similar project with the economic and social history research institute at Cologne university.
"Our project is part of a general effort to shed more light on areas that have not been fully illuminated," Degussa spokesman Wolfgang Heilmann told Reuters on Friday.

The chairwoman of the German Association for Corporate History said on Friday that firms now felt more able to tackle their uncomfortable pasts, since new, younger management teams had a less personal and emotional experience of the Nazi era.

Companies are also keen to gain public approval for acknowledging their part in the Nazi war effort. Deutsche Bank, for example, ultimately received public praise for admitting they profited from the the sale of confiscated Jewish property.
